title: Google Calendar Close Integration: Setup Without Code
summary: Google Calendar Close integration can be set up without code via Activepieces. Build a working workflow in minutes using menu-based triggers and actions.
body_markdown:
## Frequently asked questions


Once a flow is live, a handful of questions come up that the setup steps don't settle, and most of them trace back to one flow that did something unexpected.


### Can I connect Close and Google Calendar without code?


Yes. Both apps have listed triggers and actions, so a flow's built by picking steps and mapping fields. You authorize each app once.


If the Close connection asks for an API key, create it in your Close account settings and paste it in.


Use a key from an account with the access the flow needs, because a key that can't see a lead will fail on that lead without a helpful message.


### Does the integration work with more than one Google calendar?


Yes, in practice. Because the calendar's a field on the Google Calendar step, each step targets one calendar you choose. For several calendars, such as one per sales rep, add a step per calendar or run separate flows.


Don't hardcode a calendar and then forget it. The classic failure's a meeting that lands on someone's personal calendar because the field was left at its default.


### Can I self-host the workflow instead of using the cloud?


Yes, if you run the open-source edition of the automation tool. Check the integration list in your own install before you rely on it, because a self-hosted instance may lag behind the cloud version.


If a Close or Calendar step shows in the cloud builder but not on your server, update the instance before you assume the step's missing. Keep the same checklist for debugging: confirm the version, then the connection, then the field mapping.


### What should I do if the step I need isn't listed?


Call the API yourself with an HTTP request step. Authenticate it with the same credentials the app uses, point it at the endpoint in the vendor's API documentation, and map the response fields into later steps.


For the other direction, where the app should push to you, create a webhook trigger and register its URL in the app.


Test an HTTP step with a single record first. A request that returns an error still looks like a completed step in some run logs, so read the response body, not just the green check.


### Why did my workflow create the same event twice?


Almost always one of three causes. The trigger fired on an update as well as a creation. A failed step was retried after the event had already been created. Or the same flow was enabled twice, once in a test copy and once live.


Stop the duplicates by searching for an existing event before the create step, and store the Close record ID in the event description so the search has something to match. Then check that only one copy of the flow's switched on.
